title: Consensus & Leader Election
summary: How a group of servers agrees on one leader and one history — even when some of them can’t be reached.

goals.text: Why naive failover causes split brain
Majority quorums — and why they overlap
When a write counts as committed
How many nodes a cluster needs

steps.title: One leader, two followers
body: From Replication: one leader takes every write and copies it to its followers. If the leader dies, a follower is promoted and carries on.
That sentence hides one of the hardest questions in distributed systems: who decides the leader is dead — and what happens if they’re wrong?

callout.text: From the outside, a crashed server, a slow server and a server behind a broken cable all look exactly the same: silence.

steps.title: Two leaders at once
body: A network fault cuts A off from B and C. A is alive and still serving App Server 1 — but B hears nothing, assumes the leader is dead, and promotes itself.
Now two leaders accept writes. Through A, seat 7 is sold to Ana; through B, the same seat is sold to Ben. Two histories that can never be merged cleanly: split brain.

callout.text: A timeout can tell you a server is unreachable. It can never tell you the server is dead.

changes: − Network between A and the others is cut

steps.title: The rule: nothing counts without a majority
body: The fix is one rule. A leader is only elected — and a write only confirmed — when more than half of all nodes agree. With three nodes, that’s two.

Cut off, A can reach only itself: 1 of 3. It can’t confirm anything, so App Server 1’s writes wait and time out. B and C are 2 of 3: they may elect a leader and carry on. Any two majorities share at least one node, so two leaders can never both win.

callout.text: This is CAP in practice: the minority side gives up availability so that the data stays consistent.

card.title: Majority (quorum)
lines: # so only one side can ever decide

steps.title: How a leader gets elected
body: This is the Raft algorithm. A leader sends regular heartbeats. Every follower runs a timer of random length; if it runs out with no heartbeat, that follower becomes a candidate.

B’s timer fires first. It starts term 2, votes for itself and asks the others. A node gives one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as complete as its own. C says yes — 2 of 3 — so B leads term 2.

callout.text: Random timers mean two nodes rarely stand at once. If the vote does split, nobody wins, the timers restart, and the next term settles it — usually within a second.

changes: + B: no heartbeat → candidate for term 2
~ B wins 2 of 3 and starts sending heartbeats

card.title: Election · term 2
lines: # one vote per node per term

steps.title: A write is committed by a majority
body: Writes follow the same rule. App Server 2 sends seat 7 → Ben to the leader. B appends it to its log and sends it to the followers.
As soon as a majority has stored the entry — B and C — it is committed. Only then does B apply it and answer “saved”. A committed entry survives any failure that leaves a majority standing.

callout.text: Every node applies the same log entries in the same order, so every node ends up in the same state. That’s a replicated state machine — the idea underneath all of this.

changes: + B appends entry 4 to its log

steps.title: The old leader steps down
body: The network heals. A — still believing it leads term 1 — receives a heartbeat from B stamped term 2. A higher term always wins: A becomes a follower at once.

A’s log holds one entry that never reached a majority: Ana’s booking, which App Server 1 was never told had succeeded. A discards it and copies B’s log instead. All three nodes are identical again, and nothing that was confirmed has been lost.

callout.text: Terms are a logical clock. Nobody compares wall-clock times — only “whose term number is higher?”

changes: ~ A copies the log from B · apps follow the leader

steps.title: How many nodes?
body: A cluster of N nodes needs ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 votes, so it keeps working with ⌊(N − 1)/2⌋ of them down. Three nodes survive one failure; five survive two.

A fourth node is a trap: the majority becomes 3, so you still survive only one failure — with one more machine that can fail. Use odd sizes, and put each node in a different zone so one outage can’t take a majority with it.

callout.text: Three or five is typical. Every write waits for more acknowledgements as the cluster grows, so bigger clusters get slower, not safer.

steps.title: Case: the leader that paused
body: Leader B freezes for twenty seconds — a long garbage-collection pause, or its virtual machine being moved. A and C hear no heartbeats, elect C for term 3, and move on.

Then B wakes up. As far as it can tell no time has passed, and it is still the leader. Before the next message corrects it, it finishes what it was doing: writing a file to shared storage — straight over the new leader’s work.

callout.text: A node cannot know it was paused. “I checked that I was the leader a moment ago” is never proof that you still are.

changes: + A and C elect C · term 3
− B wakes up and writes as if it still led

steps.title: Fencing tokens
body: The fix doesn’t depend on B noticing anything. Every request a leader sends carries its term number as a fencing token, and the storage remembers the highest token it has seen.
C has already written with token 3. When B’s write arrives carrying token 2, the storage refuses it. The stale leader is fenced off by the resource itself.

callout.text: The same goes for distributed locks: the lock service must hand out an increasing number with each lock, and the protected resource must check it. A lock that only says “it’s yours” is not safe.

changes: + Every write carries the leader’s term
+ Storage rejects tokens older than the newest it has seen

steps.title: What consensus costs
body: Every write waits for a round trip to a majority. Inside one data center that’s a millisecond or two; with nodes in different regions it’s 50–150 ms on every write.
All writes pass through one leader, so throughput is capped by a single machine. And when no majority can be reached, the cluster accepts no writes at all — on purpose.

callout.text: Consensus buys correctness with latency and availability. Spend it on the small, critical decisions — not on every like and page view.

changes: ~ An election pauses writes for about a second

steps.title: You use it far more than you write it
body: Almost nobody implements Raft or Paxos themselves. You run a small consensus cluster — etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul — and keep only the critical facts in it: who the leader is, what the configuration says, who holds which lock.

Everything else leans on it. Kubernetes keeps all its cluster state in etcd. Kafka elects its controllers with Raft. Databases such as CockroachDB, Spanner and MongoDB run consensus inside every shard or replica set to decide failover.

callout.text: When the Replication lesson said “promote the most up-to-date follower”, this is the machinery that makes it safe.

changes: + Three systems that depend on the cluster

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A timeout can’t tell dead from unreachable — naive failover risks split brain.
  • Majority rule: elections and writes need more than half the nodes, and two majorities always overlap.
  • Terms order the leaders: a higher term wins and a stale leader steps down.
  • A write is committed once a majority has logged it — never before.
  • Run 3 or 5 nodes across zones, and use fencing tokens for anything outside the log.
